Health Melas 
*281. SHRI YADLAPATIVENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the places in the country where Government are organising health 
melas; 
(b) the rationale behind organising such melas; and 
(c) the estimated amount to be spent by Government on these melas? 
 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. 
P. THAKUR): (a) Health Melas have been organised in Mathura (U.P.), 
Delhi, Kargil (J&K) and Patna (Bihar) during the year 2000. 
State Governments have proposed Health Melas at Lucknow (U.P.), 
Ghazipur (U.P.), Imphal (Manipur), Bhopal (M.R), Guwahati (Assam) and 
Jaipur (Rajasthan). 
(b) The Health Melas aim to demons trate the need for quality health 
and family welfare services, with c onvergence and integrated delivery for 
all segments of population. 
People become aware of a number of options before them in terms of 
the different systems of medicine (a llopathy, homeopathy, ayurveda and 
unani etc.). 
1 

RAJYA SABHA   [8th December, 2000] 
People begin to comprehend the linkages between preventive, 
promotive, curative and rehabilitative health care as well as between the 
primary, secondary and tertiary health sectors. They get sensitised to the 
role of Central' Government, State Government, elected local bodies, 
NGOs and professional organisations. The pre-mela demographic and 
epidemiological surveys provide data about a given city and its rural 
hinterland. 
(c) A total cash grant of approxi mately Rs. 12.60 lakhs has been 
released by Central Government for the four health Melas held so far.

The following steps are being take n by the Government to prevent 
and control these diseases:— 
Dengue: 
1. Disease and Vector surveillance. 
2. Vector control mainly through source reduction. 
3. Early diagnosis and case management in hospitals. 
4. Information, education and communication. 
5. Early response to epidemics. 
6. Capacity building.  
        Japanese Encephalitis: 
 
• Supply of limited quantity of insecticides for vector control and 
gogging. 
• Providing technical assistance/guidance to the States to manage 
and control JE outbreaks and training of Medical Officers of PHCs 
for clinical management of JE cases and prevention of mortality. 
• Facilitating supply of Japanese Encephalitis Vaccine to the States 
from Central Research Institute Kasauli. 
HIV/AIDS:  Under the National AIDS Control Programme, which is a Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme, the main components for prevention and control of 
HIV/ 
AIDS consist of:— 
• Reducing the spread of HIV in groups at high risk by 
identification of target populati on and providing peer counselling, 
condom promotion, treatment of sexually transmitted infections. 
• Preventive intervention for the general population by Information, 
Education and Communication (IEC) and awareness campaigns, 
provision of voluntary testing and counselling, safe blood 
transfusion services and prevention of occupational exposure. 
• Providing financial assistance for treatment of opportunistic 
infections, home and community based care for persons infected 
by HIV/AIDS.

and Municipal levels.

2071. PROF. M. M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state; 
(a) whether Government have chalked out any short term and long 
term programme to make the country self reliant in the production of 
fertilizers; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the effective steps initiated by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA 
MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (d) Government  of India's policy has been to 
achieve maximum degree of attain able self-sufficiency in nitrogen 
production. In 1999-2000, the country achieved self-sufficiency to the 
extent of about 94% in the case of nitrogen. 
In the case of phosphates, the pa ucity of domestic raw material 
constrains the attainment of higher degree of self-sufficiency. 
Recognising this, a deliberate policy-mix has been adopted which 
involves modulation of three options : (i) domestic production based on 
indigenous/imported rock phosphate and imported sul phur; (ii) domestic 
production based on imported intermediates, viz. Ammonia and phosphoric 
acid; and (iii) import of finished fertilizer, viz. Di-Ammonium Phosphate 
(DAP) and complex fertilizers. In 1999-2000, about 70% of the requirement 
of phosphatic fertilizers was met through the first two options. The level of 
self-sufficiency is likely to improve further in 2000-01 with the 
contribution to phosphate fertilizer production by new plants at Paradeep 
and Dahej amounting to 17% increase in production target in 2000-01 as 
compared to actual production in 1999-2000. 
There are no known commercially exploitable reserves of potash in 
the country and the entire requirement of potassic fertilizers for direct 
application as well as for production of complex fertilizers is met 
through imports.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) According to National

prevalence of anaemia among pregnant women is over 80%. Anaemia among 
pregnant women is an important contri bbutor to low birth weight in newborn 
babies. 
Malnutrition including insufficient intake of iron and folic acid; poor 
bioavailability of iron in diet; increased requirement of iron during pregnancy; 
chronic and repeated infections and pa rasitic infestations contribute to the 
problem of anaemia among Indian women.

Improving Punctuality of Trains 
2177. PROF. M. SANKARAUNGAM: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state; 
(a) the steps taken by Government to improve the performance of trains, in 
terms of punctuality; 
(b) whether there is any strict monitoring machinery in the direction 
(c) if so, what are the findings of such machinery; and 
(d) if not, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI DIGVIAJY SINGH): (a) to (d) The following steps are being taken to 
improve the punctuality performance of trains: 
1. Holding of daily conference .by Headquarters by the General Manager 
with Heads of Departments and on the divisions by Divisional Railway 
Managers of each division on all Zonal Railways wherein detentions to 
all Mail/Express trains on the previous day as well as the current day 
are discussed, analysed and corrective action taken to enable an 
improvement in the performance. Live monitoring of trains, particularly 
those running late, is also being done at Officers level on all divisions 
and at Headquarters. 
2 All detentions to Mail/Express trains resulting in loss of punctuality 
are investigated and responsibility fixed in the Punctuality meetings 
being held daily by DRM/ADRMs on the divisions, and by AGM at 
the Headquarters level on Zonal Railways Bad cases of dentions 
resulting in serious adverse impact on punctuality of Mail/Express 
trains are separately classified at the Headquarters level and taken up 
with concerned divisions. 
3. Concerted action to control equipment failures is a regular ongoing 
exercise by the concerned departments for reducing the Track failures, 
148 

[8th December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Electric/Diesel Engine failures, C&W defects, Over Head Equipment 
failures and Signal & Telecom failures. 
4. To prevent alarm chain pulling. Instant Action Groups which include RPF, 
State Police and Commercial staff are deployed on trains which lose 
punctuality due to Alarm Chain Pulling. 
5. Running of trains at maximum permissible speed subject to observance of 
safety limits and speed restrictions. 
6. Improvement in Time tabling to provide a clear path. 
7. Liaison with State Government to tackle the Law and Orders problems and 
miscreant activities. 
The punctuality monitoring machinery of Indian railways consists of control 
cells which function round-the clock at the divisional level, Zonal Head Quarters 
level and the Railway Board level. 
The monitoring machinery keeps an on-line, real-time watch on the actual 
running of trains. 
Based on the monitoring which is being done by Railway Board, Zonal 
and Divisional levels, it is seen that the punctuality gets affected due to factors 
which are within the control of railways (equipment failures, accidents, bad 
controling etc.) as well as others on which railways have very little control. The 
latter includes alarm chain pulling, miscreant activities, agitations, law and order 
problems, bad weather, bomb blasts, natural calamities etc.
